title: Modes you can swap, rather than project types you are stuck in
goal: The question was whether the app should know what kind of thing you are making. The user's answer is that a document should not be locked into a kind: you should be able to swap between modes freely, where a mode is a preset of which panes and tool groups are showing, and you can always turn a hidden thing back on by hand and get back to what you had a second ago. Prototype that in the mocks and see whether it holds up. The thing being prototyped is one app that does four jobs, not four apps sharing a window: work made in one mode has to flow into another, so a component you drew can be put on a video timeline without leaving anything or converting anything.
notes:
REDIRECTED by the user on 2026-09-15, in their words: "regarding separate project types - i feel like if we have to, sure, but ideally you can just swap between modes without changing a document type. if you could, for example toggle the view on certain panes or tool groups manually, there's always a way to get back to the thing you had open a second ago, but if you start at a certain project mode, it's like a preset of which things are avaialable, and easy to swap between them. I think this should be considered and prototyped in the html".

So the answer to the original question is: not types, modes. A type is something a document IS and cannot easily stop being; a mode is something the WINDOW is in, and swapping costs nothing. That difference is the whole task. The document model should not learn about modes at all, which also means nothing here needs a migration.

There is already a prototype at docs/design/mocks/pages/project-kinds.html, built on the types framing. Revise it rather than starting again, and rename it if the word kind stops being true. Do not leave two prototypes arguing opposite things.

The strongest support for this direction is already in the app and should be cited: an icon frame knows it is an icon size and changes what a shape drawn in it looks like. That is context following the FRAME, not the document, which is the same instinct, and it means one document can hold an icon and a screenshot without either being in the wrong place.

The honest risk to answer rather than skip: a preset that hides a tool is indistinguishable from a broken app in the moment you reach for that tool. Every editor that has tried workspaces has had to solve 'where did my thing go'. The prototype earns its keep by showing the way back, not by showing the tidy default.

Depends on nothing new: the pane-load study (work-out-whether-the-right-hand-pane-is-carrying) is done and its findings about what the right hand pane carries are the raw material for deciding what a mode would show and hide.

SHARPENED by the user minutes later, and this is the constraint that matters most: "there is a lot of overlap between the modes so i don't want 4 separate apps with 4 different ia. I want 1 app that can do 4 jobs pretty seamlessly. You can create a component, and then show that on a video timeline".

So a mode is a LENS on one architecture, never a separate application. If the prototype ends up with a different layer list, a different panel arrangement or a different canvas per mode, it has failed, however tidy each one looks alone. The overlap the user names is the point: the same document, the same layers, the same components, seen with different things showing.

The component on a video timeline is the acid test and should be drawn first rather than last, because it is the flow most likely to break the design. It also has a real consequence worth stating: video cannot stay a separate single-clip editor if a component is to be placed on its timeline, since a component lives in the layer document and today's video editor knows nothing about that document. Say plainly in the report what that costs, because it is the bill attached to this direction.

And the chain got a third link, same conversation: "you can make an icon and use it in your component". So the flow to draw is icon into component into video timeline, in one document, with nothing converted at any step. Three links is a far harder test than one hop and a far better one: it only works if the icon, the component and the clip are all the same kind of thing to the app, which is the claim being made. Draw that chain before drawing any of the individual modes, because everything else is arranging panels and this is the part that decides whether the arrangement is even possible.

Follow the edit all the way down as well: change the icon and it should change in the component and on the timeline. A chain that only works one way, at the moment of placing, is a copy pretending to be a link, and this app already has a real answer for that in components.

A MECHANISM THE USER PROPOSED for the chain, same conversation: "maybe there are nice ways of extending history pane to show these as special types and you just use that to drag things like icons to your canvas".

SETTLED BY THE USER on 2026-09-15, after reading and rejecting an earlier two-sided framing in this task: "i don't buy your 'against' arguments. History can be global library. I think a document can contain its own stuff which can be what the library scopes to maybe."

So the split is by SCOPE, not by kind:
- History is the GLOBAL shelf. Everything you have made or captured, across documents, reachable from the menu bar with no editor window open. It is already the app-level surface that slides down over everything and survives across windows and launches, so it is the one that can carry an icon into a different document.
- The Library is the DOCUMENT's own shelf: the components, colours, text styles and effect styles this document contains.
That is a better axis than the one this task previously argued, which split by what a thing IS (captured versus made) and would have left your last screenshot and a component you built in June competing for one row. Scope answers that cleanly: they are different shelves because they reach different distances, and sorting or filtering within each is a surface detail rather than a reason for the split.

Build the prototype on that model rather than re-arguing it. The questions still genuinely open INSIDE it, which the pages should answer:
- Moving between the scopes. A component that starts as this document's and turns out to be worth keeping has to get to the global shelf, and something global dragged in has to become the document's. Show both directions and say what the gesture is.
- What a global thing is once it is placed. Dropping an icon from History into a document: is it a copy, or does it stay linked so editing the original updates every document that used it? Components already have a real answer for linking, so do not invent a second one, but DO say which applies here.
- Captures. Screenshots and recordings live in History today and are not things you 'made' in the same sense. Under this model they simply keep their place on the global shelf, so the page should show them beside icons and components and prove that reads sensibly rather than assuming it.
- Whether the Library, being the document's own contents, should just be the layers-and-assets of the document rather than a separate list, since 'a document contains its own stuff' is very close to what the layers list already shows.

EXTENSIBILITY, added by the user on 2026-09-15: "i could see the modes being extensible. some other scenarios might be 'i want to make pixel art' and we configure the setup with tools built around that".

So a mode is DATA, not a branch in the app. Four hardcoded modes would be four IAs wearing a costume, which is the thing already ruled out. The prototype should make plain what a mode is made of - which panes show, which tool groups show, what the canvas defaults to - so that pixel art is describable without anyone touching Swift.

Pixel art is a good worked example precisely because it needs more than visibility. It wants a fixed small canvas, a grid at one device pixel, nearest neighbour magnification instead of smoothing, a pencil rather than a brush, and no antialiasing on what it draws. So the question it forces is whether a mode may also CONFIGURE things rather than only show and hide them, and the answer has to be deliberate.

That is also where this direction can quietly turn back into the thing the user rejected. If swapping a mode changes how the document RENDERS, then a document is in a mode after all and swapping is no longer free. The distinction to hold: a mode may set a DEFAULT for new work and may change what the window offers, but it must not silently reinterpret what is already in the document. Say in the report where that line was drawn and show the case that tests it.

The app is already partway there and the prototype should build on it rather than invent: nearest neighbour magnification exists in the renderer (DocumentRenderer.swift:388, magnifyNearest, mirroring the canvas rule past 2x), the canvas grid is settable with its own store and settings panel (CanvasGridStore, CanvasGridSettingsView), and an icon frame already carries context that changes what a shape drawn into it looks like. Three of the ingredients of a pixel art mode are sitting there already.
acceptance: The prototype shows modes as PRESETS of what is visible, not as document types: the same document can be in any mode and nothing about the document changes when you swap
Anything made in one mode stays live in another rather than arriving as a flattened picture of itself

The crossover is shown as ONE CHAIN, because that is the test: draw an icon, use that icon inside a component, then put that component on a video timeline, with no export, no import and no conversion step anywhere along it
Editing the icon after the fact updates it everywhere down the chain: in the component, and on the timeline
One app, not four: the modes share one information architecture, and the prototype shows the SAME panels, layer list and canvas throughout rather than a different arrangement per mode
Swapping modes is quick and obvious, and the prototype shows what the window looks like in at least three of them
Anything a mode hides can be turned back on by hand, without leaving the mode, and the prototype shows how
Getting back to what you had a moment ago is always possible and is shown: no mode is a trap
It is honest about what a mode actually hides: panes, tool groups, menu items, or only some of those, stated rather than implied
The case against is answered: a person who swaps modes and finds their tool gone has been hurt, so the prototype shows what stops that feeling
It says what happens to a document made before modes existed, and what mode a new document starts in and why
A decision card is opened for the user with what the prototype found and a recommendation
Audit under queue/audits/ with the window captured in each mode, and anything rough filed as a follow-up
Where the chain's pieces are picked up from is answered, not assumed: the prototype shows the shelf a person drags an icon or a component off, and says why it is that shelf rather than the other one
Modes are an open set, not a fixed four: the prototype shows what a mode is MADE of, clearly enough that a new one could be described without changing the app
A new mode is shown being added, using pixel art as the worked example, and it is obvious from the page what had to be written down to make it exist
History is prototyped as the global shelf and the Library as the document's own, and the pages show something moving between the two scopes in both directions

Input from the comparison study that runs before this one (say-where-animating-an-icon-and-editing-a-video, page http://127.0.0.1:8791/index.html#time-compare).

The study's answer on project types, for you to agree with or argue against rather than inherit: NO types are needed to keep icon work and video work out of each other's way, because they already live in separate windows. Video is its own editor (VideoEditorState / VideoEditorView), not a lens on the layer document, so there is nothing to hide from anything.

What the study says solves the real problem instead: the surface follows the DOCUMENT rather than a kind chosen up front. A document with a duration gets a transport; a document with a repeating motion gets a cycle strip; neither has to ask what you are making before you start. That is the same shape as the weaker version already in the app, where an icon FRAME knows it is an icon size and changes what a shape drawn in it looks like.

The case that would break this and is worth testing here: the day video DOES move into the layer document, one document could hold a 24 point icon and a fourteen second recording at once, and then the question comes back with teeth. Worth saying explicitly whichever way you answer.

The revised study still lands on no project type picker, and the rebuilt mocks strengthen it rather than weaken it: motion is now a property of any layer, so an ordinary document grows a timing strip the moment something in it moves, and nothing has to be hidden from anything. See the last paragraph of the Recommendation block on time-compare.html.

ADVERSARIAL REVIEW, before writing anything. The task asks a question, so the thing to attack is the QUESTION and both of its answers, not a mock.

(1) I did not inherit the earlier study's answer. time-compare concludes 'no project type picker' but its argument is narrow: video lives in its own window, so nothing needs hiding. That argument dies the moment video moves into the layer document, which is a stated future, so it cannot carry this task on its own. I went looking for an argument that survives that day.

(2) I checked the premise of the goal against the app. 'Every tool in the app is offered on it whether or not it makes sense' is true in spirit and weaker than it sounds in fact: Tool has 17 cases and ToolBarLayout collapses them into about twelve slots by family, and almost none of them are scenario-exclusive. Select, crop, text, shapes, pen, fill and the marquee are wanted by an icon, a screen and a capture alike. The genuinely scenario-shaped things are not tools at all, they are PANELS: icon size previews, keylines, timing, auto layout, redline calipers. So a type that hides TOOLS is solving a problem the toolbar does not currently have, and the pressure is on the right hand pane, which is what work-out-whether-the-right-hand-pane-is-carrying already measured at 1052 points asked of 968 available.

(3) The strongest case FOR types, stated fairly so it can be beaten: a person drawing a 24 point glyph should not be paying attention rent on video trimming, auto layout and redline calipers, and the cheapest way to make that true is to ask what they are making at the front door. It is also a real convenience, because a kind can set the canvas size, the zoom, the grid and the export default in one click.

(4) What beats it is one fact in the app, not taste: FramePreset.all is screens PLUS icons in ONE list, frames are ordinary layers, and nothing anywhere stops a document holding a 24 point icon frame beside a 1440 point screen frame. That is the point of frames. A document-level kind then has to answer 'what kind is this document' about a document that is honestly two kinds, and every answer is wrong. I am writing a test that proves the mixed document is legal rather than asserting it.

(5) The shortest version that delivers the same value: keep the front door (a kind you pick when you start, which SETS UP the document) and throw away the gate (a kind that hides things afterwards). That is the recommendation, and it is a smaller build than either extreme.

STUDY DELIVERED. All eight acceptance items are met; what remains is the user's answer. THE ANSWER: no to the gate, yes to the front door. The app should ask what you are making, because that question can set up the canvas, zoom, guides and export in one click and today's sheet asks 'how big' instead. It must not store that answer as a KIND and use it to hide things afterwards. This is the evidence the whole argument rests on and it is run rather than asserted. - Decision card + queue/decisions/.md brief, four options, recommending a. - queue/audits/2026-09-15-project-kinds.json with three pictures of the study page. THE ARGUMENT, in the order it convinced me 1. The honest gain from hiding, counted off ToolBarLayout.bar with every Next flag on and counting 'rare' as keep: Icon 5 of 13 slots, Screen 2, Capture 0, Recording 7. Not nothing. 2. But Capture removes ZERO and capture-and-redline is the app's main real-world job, so the primary user sees no benefit at all. 3. And the Recording column describes a window that already exists: video is VideoEditorState in its own window, so it is not showing icon tools now and needs no kind to stop. The only column where hiding is both real and unsolved is Icon. 4. The crowding is not in the bar anyway. The pane study measured 1052 points asked of 968 available. A kind does nothing about that because the pane already follows the selection. 5. The decider: FramePreset.all is screens PLUS icons in one list and a frame is an ordinary layer, so ONE document holds a 24 point icon frame beside a 1440 point screen, and that is how anybody checks an icon reads at size. Ask that document what kind it is and there is no true answer. Proved rather than asserted: DocumentHasNoKindTests has isIconFrame true of the 24 and false of the 1440 in the same document, iconFrameID(containing:) returning the bell's frame for a stroke on the bell and nil for a caption on the panel, and IconStrokeWeight giving 2 inside the icon and the tool's own 4 on the screen. 6. The asymmetry of being wrong. No-kinds failing is loud, cheap and reversible and this loop already turns 'too much in here' into a task the same day. Kinds failing is silent (nobody reports a tool they never knew existed), and the kind is stored in the file, so it is a format, a migration and a promise forever. ARGUED AGAINST MYSELF, recorded so the next pass does not have to redo it: I did not inherit time-compare's answer. The argument on this page survives that day and says so explicitly in the recommendation: a document holding a fourteen second recording and a 24 point glyph is still two things, so a kind would still have no true answer, and the escape if it ever gets unbearable is a WORKSPACE (a view setting you can switch back from) rather than a property of the file. ADVERSARIAL REVIEW, before drawing anything. The thing to attack here is the IDEA, and the idea has a shared design doc arguing against it.

(1) PRODUCT-MODEL.md section 4f says in so many words: 'they are not different apps, and there is no mode to switch', and it killed the workspace switcher for modelling UI and image as modes you toggle. I did not ignore that and I did not quietly overwrite it. What 4f rejects is a lens toggle that changes the EXPERIENCE, three tabs in the title bar reading as three applications. What the user asked for is narrower: a preset of what is FOLDED, with nothing unavailable. Two of 4f's rules survive intact and the prototype holds to both: no segmented control in the title bar (the switch is a quiet popup in the window status), and the timeline appears because the document has TIME, never because of a mode. I added a dated note to 4f pointing at the prototype rather than rewriting a settled section before the user answers.

(2) The strongest thing I found is that this is half built already. PanelSectionVisibility landed this morning and its own header says: 'an override is exactly the shape a MODE will want later: a mode is a named preset of these choices, not a second mechanism'. optionalSections is nine ids, and layers/appearance/effects/the picked layer's section are not in it, so the code ALREADY refuses to let any preset hide what makes it one app. That is not a promise on a page, it is a guard, and I wrote tests that pin it.

(3) The way back is better than I expected and mostly exists. The dock's sticky Panels footer (built by ds.js on every window in the study) lists every group with a tick; the tool bar has an overflow menu; PanelSectionVisibility.Reason already distinguishes 'you turned this off' from 'nothing in this document needs it yet'. So a mode invents NO new place. That is the argument that beats the old escape-hatch objection, and it is the reason I think this is worth building rather than being a gate in disguise.

(4) One thing the mock could not just assert: .tbar-more is display:none until the window is narrow (responsive.css). A mode that folds tool groups has to make the overflow button permanent. The page forces it visible and says so rather than drawing an affordance that does not exist.

(5) The chain is the part most likely to break and it holds, for one reason: icon, component and clip are all layers, and the timeline is a view of the layers that have a start and an end. The link that carries an edit is a component, which exists. What does NOT exist is video as a layer, and that is the bill. I kept it as a separate option on the card rather than smuggling it in.

(6) Shortest version that delivers the value: modes without the video move. That is option a and it is what I recommend.

THE ANSWER THE PROTOTYPE REACHES
1. The chain works and the reason is structural: icon, component and clip are all layers, and the timeline is a view of the layers that have a start and an end. Nothing converts because there is nothing to convert into, and the edit travels because a component instance already travels.
2. The bill is real and is stated: video has to stop being VideoEditorState in its own window. That re-aims the queued video-cutting work. Modes are worth building either way, so it is a separate option on the card.
3. A mode is a named preset of PanelSectionVisibility.Choices plus tool groups plus a couple of view defaults. Not a new subsystem.
4. The line that keeps this from turning back into a document type: a mode may set a default for NEW work and may change what you are LOOKING at (grid, magnification: view settings like zoom), but may not change how existing work renders. Pixel art tests it and passes: swap into it with a smooth curve on the canvas and the curve stays smooth. Hard edges are a LAYER property, which is one small thing left to build and is not proposed here.
5. History is global, the Library is the document's. Dropping from History is a copy that FOLLOWS, which is exactly SharedComponents (decided 2026-09-09), so no second linking rule was invented.
6. Layers is where things ARE, the Library is what there IS to place. They overlap and do not merge: three placements of one bell are three layer rows and one tile, and half the Library is not layers at all.

Five layout bugs found and fixed while looking: the Follows row was using a class the inspector does not own and rendered as a giant wrapped value (now the canonical select.comp chip with Detach); the dock's sticky Panels footer covered the Library shelf until the window was given room; the moment column's qualifier ran inline because the small rule was never copied over; the chain's arrow column was too narrow and broke its caption over four lines; and the History pane had no height because .deskbody is flex with no floor, so it is now composed as the canonical .desk + .mbar + .deskbody the app-shell page uses.
